what_it_does: GPS acquisition—the initial lock onto satellite signals—is the most energy-hungry task in mobile GPS receivers. It requires computing correlations (a mathematical operation measuring signal similarity) across many possible Doppler frequency shifts and code delays, done via fast Fourier transforms (FFTs) that traditionally run at full precision to avoid loss of accuracy. This paper observes that early stages of the search can tolerate lower precision without hurting final accuracy, saving energy. It uses a mixed-radix FFT architecture (breaking the computation into mixed-size pieces) with dynamically reduced precision and ROM-assisted computing: replacing expensive multiplications with look-up tables in data regions that can tolerate rounding. The result is a GPS accelerator that acquires lock with 18.1 microjoules per fix, suitable for always-on location tracking.
